Elbow Arthritis
 CORE
November 22, 2024
Andrew R. Jensen, MD, MBE
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Learn that the different arthritides affecting the elbow have substantially different
presentations and treatment considerations.
Primary osteoarthritis of the elbow is hypertrophic in nature, most commonly presents in
manual laborers, and demonstrates a relative preservation of the ulnohumeral articular space.
It responds well to arthroscopic management; total elbow arthroplasty rarely is required.
Traditionally, inflammatory arthritides (such as rheumatoid arthritis) were the most common
indication for total elbow arthroplasty; however, with the widespread adoption of disease-
modifying antirheumatic drugs, this is no longer the case.
Posttraumatic elbow arthritis has become more common and presents a therapeutic
challenge.
Delayed onset ulnar neuritis is a potential delayed complication of arthroscopic osteocapsular
arthroplasty but can be prevented via in situ ulnar nerve decompression or transposition.





Interposition arthroplasty is a treatment option for young patients with end-stage
ulnohumeral arthritis. Instability is a common complication.
Total elbow arthroplasty may be a successful treatment option for older patients with end-
stage elbow arthritis; however, complications are more common compared with other joint
arthroplasty procedures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The various arthritides affecting the elbow have substantially different presentations,
pathophysiology, and treatment considerations.
Primary Osteoarthritis
Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology
Primary osteoarthritis of the elbow is characterized by osteophyte formation, capsular
contracture, and loose bodies. Periarticular hypertrophic osteophytes act as a
mechanical block at the end ranges of flexion and extension, causing pain.
However, there is a relative preservation of the joint space; articular cartilage loss occur
rarely occurs in patients with advanced disease. In this situation, the radiocapitellar joint
articular cartilage often is preferentially involved over ulnohumeral articular surfaces.1
Presentation

Presentation
Symptomatic primary osteoarthritis of the elbow is uncommon, affecting 2% of the
population. The average age of presentation is 50 years (range, 20 to 70 years), and men
are affected more often than women (4:1 ratio). Frequently, manual laborers are
affected, and the dominant elbow is preferentially affected.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
2/28

Patients typically present with loss of terminal flexion and extension and with painful
clicking or locking of the elbow. Pain typically is noted at the end ranges of motion but
not through the midrange, again indicating a relative preservation of the articular
cartilage.
Night pain is not typical; if present, an inflammatory cause of the arthritis should be
considered.1
Workup
Examination

Examination
Assess for prior surgical incisions and joint effusion at the lateral intracondylar fossa of
the elbow. Assess range of motion; pain usually is felt at the end ranges of flexion and
extension rather than throughout the arc. Forearm pronosupination is relatively
preserved and painless until late in the disease process.
Ulnar neuropathy is present in as many as 50% of patients; it must be carefully assessed
and documented before surgical management.1
Radiographs

Radiographs
Standard AP and lateral radiographs (Figure 1) should be obtained. Radiographs
typically demonstrate osteophyte formation at the coronoid process (anterior and
medial), coronoid fossa, radial fossa, radial head, olecranon tip, and olecranon fossa.
Joint spaces at the ulnohumeral joint usually are preserved, and joint spaces at the
radiocapitellar joint are mildly narrowed. Loose bodies may be evident; however,
radiographs typically underestimate the number that are present.1
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
3/28

Figure 1 Radiographs of an osteoarthritic elbow. AP view (A) demonstrates peripheral
osteophytes around the radial head (black arrow) and the tip of the olecranon (white
arrow), with loss of the normal contour of the olecranon fossa (broken line). Lateral view
(B) demonstrates osteophytes at the tip of the coronoid (black arrow), at the tip of the
olecranon (white arrow), and at the radial and coronoid fossae (arrowhead).
(Reproduced from Chalmers PN: Arthritis and arthroplasty of the elbow, in Lieberman JR,
ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 832-838.)
Computed Tomography

Computed Tomography
CT is useful for surgical planning; it allows for detailed assessment of osteophytes and
the presence of loose bodies.1 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction is particularly useful
in planning arthroscopic procedures (Figure 2).

9/3/26, 4:02 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
4/28

Figure 2 Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images of an elbow. The magnitude and
spatial location of bony overgrowth and loose bodies can be clearly assessed.
(Reproduced from Streubel PN, Cohen M: Open surgical release for contractures of the
elbow. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2015;23[6]:328-338.)
Management

Management
Because of the hypertrophic nature of primary osteoarthritis of the elbow, this condition
typically responds well to débridement procedures. Total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) rarely
is indicated for the management of primary osteoarthritis of the elbow. TEA is
contraindicated in patients younger than 65 years and in physically active patients
because of concerns for implant longevity.1
Inflammatory Arthritides
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
5/28

Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology
Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common inflammatory disease affecting the elbow;
others include psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Rheumatoid arthritis of the elbow presents initially as an intense synovitis that distends
the joint and causes stiffness and pain throughout the arc of motion. If synovitis persists,
secondary changes, such as fixed flexion contractures, attenuation of the soft tissues,
and ligamentous instability, develop. Ultimately, the articular cartilage becomes involved
with destruction, periarticular erosion, and cyst formation. The end result is a severely
deformed joint with loss of bone, loss of joint space, and progressive instability.1
Presentation

Presentation
Patients frequently are older and often are female. They may have a preexisting
diagnosis of inflammatory arthritis; however, this is not always the case.
On physical examination, patients will have stiffness and pain throughout range of
motion. Patients may have other involved joints that may complicate elbow surgery and
subsequent recovery (eg, wheelchair dependency, cervical spine instability).1
Workup

Workup
In addition to a standard elbow workup, the preoperative workup also should include
clinical and radiographic evaluation of the cervical spine.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
6/28

Rheumatoid arthritis is classified according to the Larsen grading system (Table 1) and
the Mayo Clinic classification system (Table 2).1
Table 1
Larsen Grading System for Rheumatoid Arthritis
Stage
Description
1
 Involves the soft tissues; near-normal radiographs
2
 Periarticular erosions and mild cartilage loss; may be evidence of soft-tissue
swelling and osteopenia on radiographs.
3
 Radiographs demonstrate marked joint-space narrowing.
4
 Advanced erosions penetrating the subchondral bone plate
5
 Radiographs demonstrate advanced joint damage and loss of articular
contour.
Reproduced from Trail IA: Arthroplasty in synovial-based arthritis of the elbow, in
Williams GR Jr, Yamaguchi K, Ramsey ML, Galatz LM, eds: Shoulder and Elbow Arthroplasty.
Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2005, pp 381-339.
Table 2
Mayo Clinic Classification of the Rheumatoid Elbow
Grade
 Description
I
 No radiographic abnormalities except periarticular osteopenia with
accompanying soft- tissue swelling. Mild to moderate synovitis generally is
present.
II
 Mild to moderate joint space reduction with minimal or no architectural
distortion.
 Recalcitrant synovitis that cannot be managed via nonsteroidal anti-
inflammatory medications alone.
III
 Variable reduction in joint space with or without cyst formation.
Architectural alteration, such as thinning of the olecranon or resorption of the
trochlea or capitellum. Synovitis is variable and may be quiescent.
IV
 Extensive articular damage with loss of subchondral bone and subluxation
or ankylosis of the joint. Synovitis may be minimal.

7/28

Data from Morrey BF, Adams RA: Semiconstrained arthroplasty for the treatment of
rheumatoid arthritis. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1992;74(4):479-490.
Management

Management
Patients with Larsen grade 1 or 2 elbows can be treated via arthroscopic osteocapsular
arthroplasty procedures, including a complete synovectomy; however, the neurovascular
anatomy may be distorted because of the disease process. Therefore, extra care must
be taken to avoid neurovascular injury.
Low demand patients and those with a Larsen grade 3 through grade 5 elbow are
candidates for TEA.1
Posttraumatic Arthritis
Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology
Articular cartilage damage occurs as a result of a traumatic injury and, at times, because
of abnormal residual anatomy with altered articular cartilage contact pressures.
Posttraumatic posteromedial rotatory instability may result in particularly rapid articular
cartilage loss if not corrected surgically.
Presentation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
8/28


Presentation
Patients often are young and have suffered prior substantial elbow trauma, including
simple or complex dislocations, distal humeral fractures, and proximal radial and ulnar
fractures. Progressive joint-space narrowing can occur months to years after traumatic
injury to the elbow (Figure 3; Resource 1). 
Figure 3 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of an elbow demonstrate posttraumatic
osteoarthritis after distal humerus fracture. (Reproduced from Sears BW, Puskas GJ,
Morrey ME, Sanchez-Sotelo J, Morrey BF: Posttraumatic elbow arthritis in the young
adult: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[11]:704-714.)
Workup

Workup
Many patients will have undergone previous surgery for the management of elbow
trauma. Therefore, previous incisions, orthopaedic hardware, and prior ulnar nerve
manipulation must be assessed. Patients also may have concomitant infection,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
9/28

particularly if the initial injury was an open injury, which requires workup and
management.
Management

Management
Consider interposition arthroplasty for younger, active patients who are unable or
unwilling to comply with the postoperative limitations of TEA (lifetime weight-lifting
restriction of less than 10 lb).2 TEA frequently is required.
Other Arthritides
Less common arthritides of the elbow include synovial chondromatosis and osteochondritis
dissecans.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Modalities
Rest, NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections, and activity modification (eg, occupation change for
laborers with primary osteoarthritis) are the mainstays of nonsurgical management.
Indications
Lack of nonsurgical management attempts and any contraindications to surgical management
(eg, active infection, lack of neuromuscular control, unwillingness or inability to comply with
postoperative limitations)1
Débridement Procedures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
10/28

Various elbow débridement procedures have been described, all of which resect osteophytes,
remove loose bodies, and débride pathologic soft tissues (synovium, capsule).
Specific elbow débridement procedures include
Osteocapsular arthroplasty
Outerbridge-Kashiwagi procedure
Column procedure
Additional considerations

Débridement Procedures
Débridement procedures for the management of elbow arthritis are associated with
excellent outcomes if the ulnohumeral joint space is preserved. The most common
elbow débridement procedure is arthroscopic osteocapsular arthroplasty. Other
procedures include the Outerbridge-Kashiwagi procedure and the column procedure.
Arthroscopic Osteocapsular Arthroplasty
This is a technically demanding arthroscopic procedure in which osteophyte excision and
capsular release are performed (Figure 4). It allows for assessment and débridement of
the entire articulation and associated procedures, such as synovectomy and loose body
removal. Relative contraindications include prior ulnar nerve transposition and prior
extensive open procedures.3
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
11/28

Figure 4 Arthroscopic image of the anterior elbow compartment obtained before
débridement during osteocapsular arthroplasty shows osteophytes (1), a thickened and
inflamed capsule with calcific deposits (2), and a loose body (3). (Reproduced from
Chalmers PN: Arthritis and arthroplasty of the elbow, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 832-838.)
Outerbridge-Kashiwagi Procedure
In this open procedure, a midline posterior approach is made to the posterior elbow
joint, and a fenestration is made connecting the olecranon and coronoid fossae.
It allows for removal of osteophytes at the olecranon tip, coronoid tip, and the olecranon
and coronoid fossae; however, limited ability exists to perform synovectomy,
capsulectomy, or address non-midline osteophytes.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
12/28

Column Procedure
This is an open procedure with medial and/or lateral incisions. Care must be taken to
preserve the collateral ligaments. Loose body removal, osteophyte resection, and
capsulectomy can be performed medially or laterally, depending on the location of the
pathology.
For elbows with less than 90o of flexion, the posterior bundle of the medial ulnar
collateral ligament should be released because it often is a tether preventing full elbow
flexion.1 In addition, the ulnar nerve should be decompressed in situ or transposed to
prevent delayed onset ulnar neuritis.
Interposition Arthroplasty
Description
In this open procedure, allograft tissue is affixed to the distal humeral articular surface,
providing a biologic interposition between the diseased articular surfaces (Figure 5). 
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
13/28

Figure 5 Intraoperative photograph of an elbow shows the use of Achilles tendon allograft during
elbow interposition arthroplasty. Three or four drill holes are created in a posterior-to-anterior
direction across the distal humerus, and the prepared graft is securely attached to the humerus
with suture through these osseous tunnels. The ulnohumeral joint is subsequently reduced over
the graft, and primary collateral ligament repair is completed. If the collaterals are deemed
insufficient, then the implanted allograft can be used to reconstruct both by threading a strand of
the graft through a single drill hole in the ulna, creating a collateral sling. (Reproduced from Sears
BW, Puskas GJ, Morrey ME, Sanchez-Sotelo J, Morrey BF: Posttraumatic elbow arthritis in the
young adult: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2012;20[11]:704-714.)
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
14/28

Interposition arthroplasty is indicated in young patients with loss of ulnohumeral joint space
who are unable or unwilling to live with the restrictions required after TEA.
Total Elbow Arthroplasty
Terminology: Linking versus constraint
Linking
Constraint
Although linked implants tend to be more highly constrained than unlinked implants, this is
not always the case.4

Total Elbow Arthroplasty
Linking is simply the physical connection between the ulnar and humeral components;
implant models are designed to be linked, unlinked, or convertible. Implants that can be
inserted in a linked or unlinked fashion are known as convertible implants.4
Highly constrained implants transmit force directly from one component to the other,
without any play between the two. Increasing constraint increases forces on the
bone/cement interfaces and, therefore, increases the rate of aseptic loosening.
Alternatively, low-constraint implants allow little inherent force transmission between
the ulnar and humeral components. Semiconstrained implants have a sloppy hinge at
the ulnohumeral interface, allowing for some movement between the two prostheses
but preventing gross instability.4 The constraint of an implant is related to but separate
from whether it is linked.
Indications

Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
15/28

Indications for TEA include patients with advanced rheumatoid arthritis of the elbow (eg,
Larsen stage 3 through stage 5), patients with unsalvageable primary ulnohumeral
arthroplasty, and low-demand patients with posttraumatic arthritis.
Historically, rheumatoid arthritis was the primary indication for TEA; however, because
of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, fewer patients with rheumatoid arthritis have
substantial elbow involvement. Acute trauma (eg, distal humeral fractures in the elderly)
is becoming a more common, nonarthritic indication for TEA.
Other Surgical Treatment Options
Isolated radiocapitellar arthritis
Options include radial head resection, anconeus interposition arthroplasty, and isolated
radiocapitellar arthroplasty (Figure 6).

9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064

Figure 6 Lateral radiograph of an elbow demonstrates partial unicompartmental radiocapitellar
joint arthroplasty. (Reproduced from Sears BW, Puskas GJ, Morrey ME, Sanchez-Sotelo J, Morrey
BF: Posttraumatic elbow arthritis in the young adult: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2012;20[11]:704-714.)
Salvage options
Distal humeral hemiarthroplasty (Figure 7) is an alternative to interposition arthroplasty.2
Arthrodesis is very rarely indicated for elbow arthritis because it precludes the ability of
bringing the hand to the face.

Surgical Techniques and Pearls
Arthroscopic Osteocapsular Arthroplasty
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
18/28

Positioning
Preventing neurologic injury is of paramount concern.
Osteophytectomy
Capsulectomy
Postoperative management

Arthroscopic Osteocapsular Arthroplasty
The patient may be positioned supine, lateral, or prone for elbow arthroscopy according
to surgeon preference (Figure 8). A sterile tourniquet often is used. 
Figure 8 Intraoperative photograph shows a patient in the lateral decubitus position.
The surgical arm is positioned in an arm holder such that the arm may be draped freely
to allow for complete access to the elbow. (Image courtesy of Scott P. Steinmann, MD,
Rochester, MN.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
19/28

Nerves at risk during portal placement, débridement, and capsular release include the
median nerve (anteromedial), the ulnar nerve (posteromedial), and the radial nerve (lies
anterior to the anterolateral capsule). Joint distention moves the capsule away from
bone; however, the distance between the neurovascular structures and the capsule
remain unchanged. Therefore, the nerves remain at risk during capsular work.1 The use
of arthroscopic retractors improves the field of view and, therefore, the safety of the
procedure.5
To decrease the risk of neurologic injury, the Safety-Drive Strategy has been described
by Blonna et al.5 The four steps of this strategy are: get in and establish a view, create a
space in which to work, bone removal, and capsulectomy.
The olecranon fossa is an oval structure that is wider in the medial to lateral dimension.
Olecranon and coronoid osteophytes extend medially and laterally and not just at the
tip. The coronoid and the radial fossae must be restored to improve flexion.
This is performed after osteophyte removal to prevent the egress of arthroscopic fluid
into the surrounding tissues. Some surgeons choose to perform capsulotomies or partial
capsulectomies rather than complete capsulectomies.
Early active range of motion or continuous passive motion is critical to prevent recurrent
stiffness. Pharmacologic prophylaxis for heterotopic ossification typically is not
prescribed; however, it may be used at the discretion of the surgeon1 (Video 1;
Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064

Video 1 Steinmann SP: The stiff elbow: Arthroscopic management of elbow arthritis and
elbow arthrofibrosis, in Field LH, Steinmann SP, eds: Arthroscopic Surgical Techniques:

Interposition Arthroplasty
Surgical Approach
Approaches are similar to those used for TEA. Regardless of approach, contracted capsular
tissue must be released off the anterior and posterior aspects of the distal humerus to safely
dislocate the elbow.
Interposition
If the distal humerus articular surface is fully exposed, all remaining articular cartilage is
removed but the subchondral bone is preserved. An Achilles tendon allograft is wrapped over
the distal humerus and affixed with nonabsorbable suture via bone tunnels. The elbow is then
reduced.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
21/28

Preventing instability
The tails of the allograft tissue can be used to augment stability; however, collateral ligament
repair is critical to successful outcomes. An external fixator may be required if the elbow is
unstable.
Total Elbow Arthroplasty
Surgical Approach
Surgical approaches for TEA are categorized according to extensor mechanism management.

Surgical Approach
Broadly, approaches are available for patients in whom the extensor mechanism is left
intact and patients in whom the extensor mechanism is violated and then subsequently
repaired.
Extensor mechanism–preserving approaches include the paraolecranon and the Alonso-
Llames bilaterotricipital (also known as paratricipital) approaches.6 Visualization,
particularly for ulnar instrumentation, may be more difficult during these approaches;
however, no risk of postoperative triceps rupture exists, and patients may be able to
begin postoperative range of motion exercises sooner.
Extensor mechanism–violating approaches include the Bryan-Morrey, triceps fascial
tongue, diamond pop-up, and digastric olecranon osteotomy approaches among many
others.6 These approaches allow for better visualization and easier instrumentation;
however, the extensor mechanism must heal postoperatively.
Implants
After the elbow joint is dislocated, the ulna and humerus are prepared, and implants are
trialed. As previously mentioned, these implants may be linked, unlinked, or convertible,
depending on implant design.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
22/28

Some implant systems have optional radial head arthroplasties, whereas other systems
maintain or excise the radial head. Most implants use cement fixation for the ulnar and
humeral components. Ligament repair is critical, especially if an unlinked prosthesis is used.
Postoperative management
For extensor mechanism–violating approaches, postoperative range of motion typically is
delayed. Regardless of the surgical approach, patients must comply with a lifetime weight-
lifting restriction of less than 10 lb.
Outcomes and Complications
Débridement Procedures
Outcomes

Outcomes
A recent systematic review found that open and arthroscopic débridement procedures
are as effective as open procedures with regard to improving pain scores, range of
motion arcs, and functional outcomes in patients with primary osteoarthritis; however,
open procedures are associated with higher complication and revision surgery rates.7
Complications

Complications
Complications include neurologic injury, infection, heterotopic ossification, hematoma,
and stiffness.
A series of 502 arthroscopic elbow osteocapsular arthroplasty procedures reported a 5%
incidence of transient nerve injury. All nerve injuries resolved without intervention.
Prolonged tourniquet time may be a cause of transient postoperative nerve injury. In
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
23/28

one study, the mean tourniquet time was 176 minutes in patients with tourniquet-
related nerve palsies versus 95 minutes in those without this complication.5
Infections may manifest as superficial (minor wound complications) or deep; deep
infections are more common in the elbow than in other joints managed
arthroscopically.1
Interposition Arthroplasty
Outcomes
Neither complete pain relief nor complete function should be anticipated; however, patients
do not have to comply with the same postoperative restrictions required after TEA.2
Preoperative elbow instability is associated with poorer postoperative outcomes after
interposition arthroplasty
Complications
The number 1 cause of failure after interposition arthroplasty is elbow instability.2 Progressive
ulnar or humeral bone loss is possible. Failed elbow interposition arthroplasty can be revised
to TEA.
Total Elbow Arthroplasty
Outcomes

Outcomes
A study of 461 TEA procedures in patients with rheumatoid arthritis reported that
implant survival was 92% at 10 years postoperatively, 83% at 15 years postoperatively,
and 68% at 20 years postoperatively.8
Few studies have evaluated the outcomes of TEA in patients with noninflammatory
conditions; however, small studies on TEA in patients with posttraumatic elbow arthritis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001064
24/28

have reported that short-term to midterm revision surgery rates are as high as 20% to
25%.9 (Resource 3).
Complications

Complications
Complications include infection, instability, aseptic loosening, wound healing problems,
ulnar neuropathy, periprosthetic fracture, bushing wear, and triceps insufficiency.4
Aseptic loosening and bushing wear are complications of constrained and
semiconstrained implants. Triceps insufficiency may cause pain and weakness, and
implant instability if an unlinked implant was used.
Wound healing often is an issue because the skin may be of poor quality and atrophic as
a result of long-term corticosteroid use, such as in patients with inflammatory arthritis.1
